title: Without minimums, residents' cars spill onto surrounding streets and crowd out existing residents
oneLiner: If the building does not house the cars, the street does.
body: Residents of new developments will own cars at roughly the rate of their neighbours, whatever the building provides. Opponents of removal argue the predictable result is competition for kerbside space that existing residents regard as theirs.
contextBackground: This is the objection that fills council meetings. It is a real cost; the question is whether it is the council's problem to solve through the building or through the street.
contextDisagreement: Supporters of removal generally concede spillover occurs where street parking is free and unmanaged, and argue the remedy is to manage the street. Opponents regard that as shifting a cost onto existing residents who did not choose it.

otherClaim.title: Councils should abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing

claimItself.title: Councils should abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether planning schemes should stop requiring a set number of car spaces per new dwelling and let builders decide.
claimItself.body: Most Australian planning schemes require new apartments and townhouses to include a minimum number of off-street car spaces, typically one or more per dwelling. The proposal removes the minimum. Developers could still build parking; they would no longer be required to.

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Parking minimums add roughly $70,000 to the cost of a two-bedroom apartment in Sydney, $62,000 in Melbourne and up to $137,000 in Perth

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Auckland removed minimum parking requirements citywide in 2016, and new developments near frequent transit have since provided markedly less parking

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: New housing completions have not kept pace with population growth in Australia's largest cities over the past decade

usedIn.relationSentence: This claim contradicts “Councils should abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing”

strengthDefinitions.tangential: True perhaps, but it does not land against this claim.

otherClaim.title: Up to 40 per cent of residential and on-street parking in inner Melbourne sits empty at night, and most street spaces are used by residents who already have off-street parking

claimItself.title: Up to 40 per cent of residential and on-street parking in inner Melbourne sits empty at night, and most street spaces are used by residents who already have off-street parking
claimItself.oneLiner: The spillover fear meets the occupancy data.
claimItself.body: Victoria's government cited up to 40 per cent of inner-Melbourne residential car parks sitting empty when it changed its rules, and Grattan's report found a similar share of on-street spaces vacant overnight, with most of the occupied ones used by residents who also have a garage or driveway. If the street is that underused, new residents' cars have somewhere to go.

otherClaim.title: Councils can manage street parking with permits and pricing, independently of what new buildings provide

claimItself.title: Councils can manage street parking with permits and pricing, independently of what new buildings provide
claimItself.oneLiner: Kerbside space is the council's to allocate; it does not have to be first-come, first-served.
claimItself.body: Resident permit schemes, time limits and paid parking are standard tools and are already used in most inner suburbs. They address street crowding directly, whatever the parking provision in new buildings, and can be introduced in the same decision that removes the minimum.
